title: Polar Form, De Moivre's Theorem & Roots of Unity

questions.q: Write $z=1+\sqrt{3}i$ in polar form $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, giving the argument in radians.
questions.answer: $r=\sqrt{1^2+(\sqrt{3})^2}=\sqrt{1+3}=2$. $\theta=\arctan\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (first quadrant). Polar form: $z=2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

questions.q: Convert $z=4\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ to Cartesian form $a+bi$.
questions.answer: $a=4\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=4\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=-2\sqrt{3}$. $b=4\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=4\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=2$. So $z=-2\sqrt{3}+2i$.

sections.heading: Multiplying and dividing in polar form

questions.q: Given $z_1=3\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and $z_2=2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, find $z_1z_2$ in polar form.
questions.answer: Multiply moduli, add arguments: $z_1z_2=3(2)\left(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+i\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)=6\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12}+i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)$.

questions.q: Using the same $z_1$ and $z_2$, find $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}$ in polar form.
questions.answer: Divide moduli, subtract arguments: $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=\dfrac{3}{2}\left(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+i\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)=\dfrac{3}{2}\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$.

questions.q: State De Moivre's theorem, and use it to find $\left[2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]^4$.
questions.answer: De Moivre's theorem: $[r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)]^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta)$. Applying it: $2^4\left(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{6}\right)=16\left(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=16\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\right)=-8+8\sqrt{3}i$.

questions.q: Use De Moivre's theorem to find $(1+i)^6$, giving your answer in Cartesian form.
questions.answer: Convert to polar: $|1+i|=\sqrt{2}$, $\arg(1+i)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. So $(1+i)^6=(\sqrt{2})^6\left(\cos\dfrac{6\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{6\pi}{4}\right)=8\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)=8(0-i)=-8i$.

questions.q: Find the three cube roots of $z=8\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, giving arguments in $[0,2\pi)$.
questions.answer: The cube roots have modulus $8^{1/3}=2$ and arguments $\dfrac{\pi/2+2\pi k}{3}$ for $k=0,1,2$: $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, and $\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$. So the roots are $2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, $2\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$, and $2\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)$.

questions.q: Find all four fourth roots of unity (solutions to $z^4=1$), and explain their geometric arrangement on the Argand diagram.
questions.answer: Writing $1=\cos0+i\sin0$, the roots have modulus 1 and arguments $\dfrac{2\pi k}{4}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$: $\theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, giving $z=1,i,-1,-i$. Geometrically, these four points lie evenly spaced around the unit circle, forming the vertices of a square.

sections.heading: Using De Moivre's theorem to derive trig identities

questions.q: Use De Moivre's theorem with $n=2$ to express $\cos2\theta$ in terms of $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$, by expanding $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^2$ and comparing real parts.
questions.answer: $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^2=\cos^2\theta+2i\cos\theta\sin\theta+i^2\sin^2\theta=(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)+i(2\sin\theta\cos\theta)$. By De Moivre's theorem, this also equals $\cos2\theta+i\sin2\theta$. Comparing real parts: $\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta$.

questions.q: Using the same expansion from the previous problem, compare imaginary parts to find an identity for $\sin2\theta$.
questions.answer: Comparing imaginary parts of $(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)+i(2\sin\theta\cos\theta)=\cos2\theta+i\sin2\theta$: $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$.

sections.heading: Roots of a general complex number

questions.q: Find the two square roots of $z=-4$, giving your answers in Cartesian form.
questions.answer: Write $-4=4(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi)$. Square roots have modulus $4^{1/2}=2$ and arguments $\dfrac{\pi+2\pi k}{2}$ for $k=0,1$: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$. Roots: $2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=2i$, and $2\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)=-2i$.

questions.q: Solve the equation $z^3=-8i$, giving all three roots in polar form with arguments in $[0,2\pi)$.
questions.answer: Write $-8i=8\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)$. Cube roots have modulus $8^{1/3}=2$ and arguments $\dfrac{3\pi/2+2\pi k}{3}$ for $k=0,1,2$: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$, $\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$. Roots: $2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $2\left(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)$, $2\left(\cos\dfrac{11\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\right)$.

sections.heading: Applying De Moivre's theorem to negative and fractional powers

questions.q: Find $z^{-3}$ for $z=2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$, using the extended form of De Moivre's theorem for negative integer powers.
questions.answer: De Moivre's theorem extends to negative integers: $z^{-3}=2^{-3}\left(\cos\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)+i\sin\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)\right)=\dfrac{1}{8}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}i\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{16}-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{16}i$.

questions.q: Sum the four fourth roots of unity found earlier in this worksheet ($1,i,-1,-i$), and explain the general result this illustrates about the sum of all $n$th roots of unity for $n\geq2$.
questions.answer: $1+i+(-1)+(-i)=0$. In general, the sum of all $n$ distinct $n$th roots of unity is always $0$ for $n\geq2$, since the roots are evenly and symmetrically spaced around the unit circle, causing their vector sum to cancel completely.

sections.heading: Solving equations that reduce to roots of unity

questions.q: Solve $(z+1)^4=1$ for $z$, by first finding the fourth roots of unity and then solving for $z$.
questions.answer: The fourth roots of unity are $w=1,i,-1,-i$ (found earlier). Setting $z+1=w$: $z=w-1$, giving $z=0,\ i-1,\ -2,\ -i-1$.

questions.q: Find the modulus and argument of $z=\dfrac{(1+i)^3}{1-i}$, using De Moivre's theorem for the numerator and standard polar division for the quotient.
questions.answer: $1+i$ has modulus $\sqrt{2}$ and argument $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $(1+i)^3$ has modulus $(\sqrt{2})^3=2\sqrt{2}$ and argument $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$. $1-i$ has modulus $\sqrt{2}$ and argument $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Dividing: modulus $=\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=2$; argument $=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\pi$. So $z$ has modulus $2$ and argument $\pi$.

sections.heading: Using De Moivre's theorem for a triple-angle identity

questions.q: Use De Moivre's theorem with $n=3$ to express $\cos3\theta$ in terms of $\cos\theta$, by expanding $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3$ and comparing real parts.
questions.answer: $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3=\cos^3\theta+3i\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta-i\sin^3\theta$. The real part is $\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$. By De Moivre's theorem, this equals $\cos3\theta$. Substituting $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$: $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta(1-\cos^2\theta)=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$.

questions.q: Find the six sixth roots of unity, and state which of these roots are also fourth roots of unity.
questions.answer: The sixth roots of unity have modulus $1$ and arguments $\dfrac{2\pi k}{6}=\dfrac{\pi k}{3}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4,5$: $0,\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\pi,\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, giving $z=1,\ \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i,\ -\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i,\ -1,\ -\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i,\ \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i$. The fourth roots of unity are $1,i,-1,-i$. Comparing the two lists, only $z=1$ and $z=-1$ appear in both — these are the roots common to both sets, since they correspond to arguments that are multiples of both $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (i.e. multiples of $\pi$).

sections.heading: Applying De Moivre's theorem to solve an equation with a shifted variable

questions.q: Solve $z^5=32$ for $z$, giving all five roots in polar form with arguments in $[0,2\pi)$.
questions.answer: Write $32=32(\cos0+i\sin0)$. The fifth roots have modulus $32^{1/5}=2$ and arguments $\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$: $0,\dfrac{2\pi}{5},\dfrac{4\pi}{5},\dfrac{6\pi}{5},\dfrac{8\pi}{5}$. Roots: $2\left(\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}+i\sin\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}\right)$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$, i.e. $2,\ 2\left(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+i\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right),\ 2\left(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}+i\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\right),\ 2\left(\cos\dfrac{6\pi}{5}+i\sin\dfrac{6\pi}{5}\right),\ 2\left(\cos\dfrac{8\pi}{5}+i\sin\dfrac{8\pi}{5}\right)$.

sections.heading: Combining polar arithmetic with De Moivre's theorem

questions.q: Given $z_1=\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$, find $z_1^8$ in its simplest Cartesian form, and explain why the result is a positive real number.
questions.answer: By De Moivre's theorem: $z_1^8=(\sqrt{2})^8\left(\cos\dfrac{8\pi}{4}+i\sin\dfrac{8\pi}{4}\right)=16(\cos2\pi+i\sin2\pi)=16(1+0i)=16$. The result is a positive real number because the argument $\dfrac{8\pi}{4}=2\pi$ is a full rotation, landing back on the positive real axis where $\sin=0$ and $\cos=1$.
